line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 Bxc6 dxc6
teaches: Doubled pawns are only weak when they cover nothing — before recapturing, look at which squares each pawn would hold from its new file, because a doubled pawn that takes away the two squares the opponent's pieces most want has already paid for the cosmetic damage.
explains: The bishop has been traded for the knight and the pawn recaptures toward the centre. From c6 that pawn covers b5 and d5 — the outpost square in the middle and the square on the wing where a bishop or knight would otherwise sit and annoy. The pawns look untidy on the c-file and the position is perfectly sound, because the squares that matter are held.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 Bxc6 dxc6 d3
teaches: When you have given up the bishop pair, do not rush to open the position — the modest one-square pawn move keeps the centre closed enough that the two bishops have nothing to aim at, and time spent making the position solid is time the opponent cannot spend making it sharp.
explains: The pawn steps only to d3 rather than to d4. It props up the pawn on e4 so the centre cannot be undermined, and covers c4 so no piece drops in there. The position stays closed while the pieces come out — which is exactly what the side without the bishop pair wants.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 Bxc6 dxc6 d3 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3
teaches: When two pieces can recapture, take with the one that lands doing something — a queen that arrives hitting a piece has gained the move the recapture would normally cost, and if she also sits behind her own pawns she is safe from being chased off again.
explains: The bishop has been traded on f3 and the queen takes back. From f3 she hits the knight on f6 immediately, so the recapture comes with a question attached rather than as a pause. She also stands behind the pawns on d3, e4, g2 and h3, which means there is no square from which she can be harassed.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 Bxc6 dxc6 d3 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Nd7 Be3 e5 a4
teaches: In a closed position the pawn breaks are the only way in, so the strongest prophylactic move is often the one that takes a break square away before the break is prepared — a pawn spent on the wing costs nothing here, and the plan it stops was the opponent's only one.
explains: The centre is locked with pawns on e4 and e5 and neither side can force it open there. The pawn goes to a4 and covers b5, which is the square the queenside pawn break needs. With that square held, the position has no natural way to be opened, and the game becomes about who can improve their worst piece.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 Bxc6 dxc6 d3 Bg7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 Nd7 Be3 e5 a4 a5 Ne2
teaches: In a locked position a knight that has run out of squares should retreat toward a route rather than stand still — judge the retreat by where it can go next and by what it holds on the way, because a knight stepping back while still covering the key central square has lost nothing at all.
explains: With the pawns fixed, the knight on c3 has nothing left to do there. Dropping back to e2 keeps it covering d4, the one central square either side could use as an outpost, and opens the route toward the kingside where the position is not yet decided. Retreating is not passive when the square behind is a crossroads.
